units.title: Module 1: Development of practical skills in chemistry

topics.title: 1.1 Practical skills assessed in a written examination

outcomes.text: Design experiments, including solving problems in a practical context and choosing suitable apparatus and techniques.
Identify the variables that must be controlled.
Evaluate whether an experimental method suits the expected outcomes.
Use a wide range of practical apparatus and techniques correctly.
Use appropriate units for measurements.
Present observations and data in a suitable format.
Process, analyse and interpret qualitative and quantitative results.
Use suitable mathematical skills to analyse quantitative data.
Use significant figures appropriately.
Plot and interpret graphs, choosing axes and scales and measuring gradients and intercepts.
Evaluate results and draw conclusions.
Identify anomalies in measurements.
Identify limitations in experimental procedures.
Judge precision and accuracy, including margins of error, percentage errors and apparatus uncertainties.
Suggest improvements to procedures and apparatus.

topics.title: 1.2 Practical skills assessed in the practical endorsement

outcomes.text: Apply investigative approaches and methods to practical work.
Use practical equipment and materials safely and correctly, identifying hazards and minimising risks.
Follow written instructions.
Make and record observations and measurements.
Keep appropriate records of experimental activities.
Present information and data scientifically.
Use software and tools to process data, research and report findings.
Use online and offline research skills across websites, textbooks and printed sources.
Cite sources of information correctly.
Use a wide range of experimental instruments, equipment and techniques.
Use apparatus to record mass, time, volume of liquids and gases, and temperature.
Heat using a water bath, electric heater or sand bath.
Measure pH using charts, a pH meter or a probe on a data logger.
Carry out titration, distillation and reflux, qualitative tests for ions and organic groups, and filtration.
Use a volumetric flask to make up a standard solution.
Use acid-base indicators in titrations of weak and strong acids and alkalis.
Purify a solid by recrystallisation and a liquid using a separating funnel.
Use melting point apparatus.
Use thin layer or paper chromatography.
Set up electrochemical cells and measure voltages.
Handle solids and liquids safely, including corrosive, irritant, flammable and toxic substances.
Measure rates of reaction by at least two methods, such as initial rate and continuous monitoring.
Define isotopes as atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons.
Describe atomic structure in terms of protons, neutrons and electrons for atoms and ions.
Define relative isotopic mass and relative atomic mass against carbon-12.
Use mass spectrometry data to find isotopic masses, abundances and relative atomic mass.
Calculate relative molecular mass and relative formula mass.
Write formulae of ionic compounds from ionic charges, predicting charges from the periodic table and recalling common ions.
Construct balanced equations, including ionic equations and state symbols, for known and unfamiliar reactions.
Explain and use amount of substance, the mole, the Avogadro constant, molar mass and molar gas volume.
Use the terms empirical formula and molecular formula.
Calculate empirical and molecular formulae from composition by mass or percentage.
Use the terms anhydrous, hydrated and water of crystallisation and calculate hydrated salt formulae.
Calculate with amount of substance involving mass, gas volume, and solution volume and concentration.
Use the ideal gas equation pV = nRT.
Use stoichiometric relationships in calculations.
Calculate percentage yield.
Calculate atom economy.
Carry out techniques for measuring mass, solution volumes and gas volumes.
Explain the sustainability benefits of high atom economy processes.
Give formulae of common acids and alkalis and explain that acids release H+ and alkalis release OH- in water.
Explain strong and weak acids in terms of relative dissociation.
Describe neutralisation of acids with bases, carbonates, metal oxides and alkalis to form salts, with full equations.
Prepare a standard solution and carry out acid-base titrations.
Do structured and unstructured titration calculations for familiar and unfamiliar acids and bases.
Assign and calculate oxidation numbers for atoms in elements, compounds and ions.
Write formulae using oxidation numbers.
Use Roman numerals to show oxidation number magnitude.
Describe oxidation and reduction as electron transfer and as changes in oxidation number.
Describe redox reactions of metals with acids to form salts, with full equations.
Interpret redox equations, including unfamiliar ones, in terms of oxidation numbers and electron loss or gain.
State how many electrons fill the first four shells.
Describe atomic orbitals as regions holding up to two electrons of opposite spin, with the shapes of s- and p-orbitals and the numbers of orbitals in s, p and d sub-shells.
Fill orbitals in order of increasing energy, occupying equal-energy orbitals singly before pairing.
Deduce electron configurations of atoms up to Z = 36.
Deduce electron configurations of s- and p-block ions up to Z = 36.
Explain ionic bonding as electrostatic attraction and draw dot-and-cross diagrams.
Explain giant ionic lattice structures such as NaCl.
Explain how structure and bonding affect melting and boiling points, solubility and conductivity of ionic compounds.
Explain a covalent bond as attraction between a shared electron pair and the nuclei.
Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for single, multiple and dative covalent bonding.
Use average bond enthalpy as a measure of covalent bond strength.
Predict shapes and bond angles for up to six electron pairs using electron pair repulsion, including lone pair repulsion.
Explain linear, non-linear, trigonal planar, pyramidal, tetrahedral and octahedral shapes.
Define electronegativity and interpret Pauling values.
Explain polar bonds, permanent dipoles and polar molecules in terms of shape.
Explain intermolecular forces from permanent and induced dipole interactions.
Explain hydrogen bonding between molecules containing N, O or F and H.
Explain anomalous properties of water caused by hydrogen bonding.
Explain simple molecular lattices such as iodine and ice.
Describe the periodic table as elements arranged by proton number, with periodic trends in periods and similar properties in groups.
Describe the trend in electron configurations across Periods 2 and 3 and classify elements into s-, p- and d-blocks.
Define first ionisation energy and explain trends across Periods 2 and 3 and down a group.
Predict from successive ionisation energies the electrons per shell and the group of an element.
Explain metallic bonding and the giant metallic lattice.
Explain giant covalent lattices of diamond, graphite, graphene and silicon.
Explain physical properties of giant metallic and giant covalent lattices.
Explain the variation in melting points across Periods 2 and 3 in terms of structure and bonding.
Explain Group 2 outer s2 configuration and loss of electrons to form 2+ ions in redox reactions.
Compare the reactivity of Mg to Ba with oxygen, water and dilute acids.
Explain the reactivity trend in terms of first and second ionisation energies.
Describe the action of water on Group 2 oxides and the pH trend of the solutions.
Describe uses of Group 2 compounds as bases, such as Ca(OH)2 for soil and Mg(OH)2 and CaCO3 as antacids, with equations.
Explain the boiling point trend of Cl2, Br2 and I2 using London forces.
Describe the s2p5 configuration and the gain of one electron to form 1- ions.
Describe the reactivity trend of Cl2, Br2 and I2 in displacement of halide ions.
Explain the reactivity trend in terms of attraction, atomic radius and shielding.
Explain disproportionation using chlorine with water and with cold dilute sodium hydroxide.
Weigh the benefits and risks of chlorine in water treatment.
Describe precipitation of Cl-, Br- and I- with silver ions followed by ammonia as a halide test.
Identify carbonate, sulfate and halide anions with the correct sequence of tests.
Identify ammonium ions by warming with sodium hydroxide.
Explain exothermic and endothermic reactions and the sign of enthalpy change.
Draw enthalpy profile diagrams.
Explain activation energy qualitatively.
Define standard conditions and enthalpy changes of reaction, formation, combustion and neutralisation.
Determine enthalpy changes from experimental results using q = mcDT.
Describe techniques for determining enthalpy changes directly and indirectly.
Explain average bond enthalpy as bond breaking in gaseous molecules.
Explain exothermic and endothermic reactions through bond breaking and making.
Use average bond enthalpies to calculate enthalpy changes.
Use Hess's law and enthalpy cycles to find reaction enthalpies from combustion data.
Use enthalpy cycles to find reaction enthalpies from formation data.
Use unfamiliar enthalpy cycles.
Explain the effect of concentration and gas pressure on rate through collision frequency.
Calculate reaction rate from gradients of graphs.
Describe techniques for investigating rates by measuring mass, gas volume and time.
Explain how a catalyst speeds up a reaction by a lower activation energy route without being used up.
Explain homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts.
Explain the economic and sustainability benefits of catalysts.
Explain the Boltzmann distribution and its link to activation energy.
Use Boltzmann distributions to explain the effect of temperature and catalysts on rate.
Explain dynamic equilibrium in a closed system.
Apply le Chatelier's principle to changes in temperature, pressure and concentration.
Explain that a catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium.
Describe techniques for investigating equilibrium shifts.
Explain the compromise between equilibrium and rate in industrial conditions.
Write expressions for Kc and calculate Kc from equilibrium concentrations.
Estimate the position of equilibrium from the size of Kc.
Apply IUPAC rules to name organic compounds systematically.
Use general, structural, displayed and skeletal formulae.
Define and use homologous series, functional group, alkyl, aliphatic, alicyclic, aromatic, saturated and unsaturated.
Use the general formula of a homologous series to predict member formulae.
Explain structural isomers and deduce possible structures from a molecular formula.
Describe homolytic and heterolytic fission.
Explain radicals and show them with dots in mechanisms.
Describe a curly arrow as movement of an electron pair.
Draw reaction mechanisms with curly arrows and dipoles.
Describe alkanes as saturated hydrocarbons with sigma bonds and free rotation.
Explain the tetrahedral shape around carbon in alkanes.
Explain boiling point variation with chain length and branching.
Explain the low reactivity of alkanes through bond enthalpy and low polarity.
Describe complete and incomplete combustion of alkanes and the danger of CO.
Describe radical substitution with halogens: initiation, propagation and termination.
Explain the limitations of radical substitution in synthesis.
Describe alkenes as unsaturated hydrocarbons with a pi-bond and a sigma-bond, and restricted rotation.
Explain the trigonal planar shape around C=C.
Explain stereoisomers, E/Z isomerism and cis-trans isomerism.
Use CIP priority rules to identify E and Z isomers.
Determine possible E/Z isomers from a structural formula.
Explain alkene reactivity through the low bond enthalpy of the pi-bond.
Describe addition of hydrogen, halogens, hydrogen halides and steam, including the bromine test.
Define an electrophile.
Describe the mechanism of electrophilic addition.
Use Markownikoff's rule and carbocation stability to predict major products.
Deduce the repeat unit of an addition polymer from its monomer and the monomer from a polymer section.
Explain sustainability benefits of processing waste polymers by combustion, feedstock recycling and removing toxic products.
Explain the benefits of biodegradable and photodegradable polymers.
Explain alcohol polarity, water solubility and low volatility using hydrogen bonding.
Classify alcohols as primary, secondary or tertiary.
Describe combustion of alcohols.
Describe oxidation of primary alcohols to aldehydes and carboxylic acids with controlled conditions.
Describe oxidation of secondary alcohols to ketones and the resistance of tertiary alcohols.
Describe acid-catalysed elimination of water from alcohols to form alkenes.
Describe substitution of alcohols with halide ions in acid to form haloalkanes.
Describe hydrolysis of haloalkanes by aqueous alkali and by water with silver nitrate, comparing rates.
Define a nucleophile.
Describe the mechanism of nucleophilic substitution in hydrolysis of primary haloalkanes.
Explain the hydrolysis rate trend using carbon-halogen bond enthalpies.
Explain how UV light produces halogen radicals from CFCs and catalyses the breakdown of ozone, with equations.
Use Quickfit apparatus for distillation and heating under reflux.
Prepare and purify an organic liquid using a separating funnel, drying agents and redistillation.
Identify functional groups in a molecule and predict its properties and reactions.
Devise two-stage synthetic routes between the functional groups studied.
Explain that infrared radiation makes covalent bonds vibrate and absorb energy.
Explain absorption of infrared by atmospheric gases and the link to global warming.
Identify alcohols, aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids from infrared absorption peaks.
Interpret and predict infrared spectra using supplied data.
Describe use of infrared to monitor air pollution gases and in breathalysers.
Use a mass spectrum to identify the molecular ion peak and molecular mass.
Analyse fragmentation peaks to suggest fragment structures.
Deduce structures of organic compounds from elemental analysis, mass spectra and infrared spectra.

units.title: Module 5: Physical chemistry and transition elements

outcomes.text: Explain and use rate of reaction, order, overall order, rate constant, half-life and rate-determining step.
Deduce orders from experimental data and write a rate equation.
Calculate the rate constant and its units from a rate equation.
Deduce zero or first order from the shape of a concentration-time graph and calculate rates from gradients.
Measure the constant half-life of a first order reaction and use k = ln2/t1/2.
Deduce order from a rate-concentration graph and find k for a first order reaction from the gradient.
Describe initial rates and continuous monitoring methods, including colorimetry.
Predict a rate equation consistent with the rate-determining step, and possible mechanism steps from a rate equation.
Explain qualitatively how temperature changes the rate constant.
Use the Arrhenius equation and find Ea and A graphically from ln k against 1/T.
Use mole fraction and partial pressure.
Calculate quantities present at equilibrium from data.
Describe techniques to determine quantities present at equilibrium.
Write Kc and Kp expressions for homogeneous and heterogeneous equilibria.
Calculate Kc and Kp, including units.
Describe how temperature changes equilibrium constants for exothermic and endothermic reactions.
Explain that equilibrium constants do not change with concentration, pressure or catalyst.
Explain how an equilibrium constant controls the position of equilibrium.
Apply these principles to other equilibrium constants.
Define Bronsted-Lowry acids and bases, conjugate pairs, and monobasic, dibasic and tribasic acids.
Explain the role of H+ in reactions of acids with metals and bases using ionic equations.
Use the acid dissociation constant Ka and pKa.
Use pH = -log[H+] and [H+] = 10^-pH.
Use the ionic product of water, Kw.
Calculate pH for strong monobasic acids and strong bases.
Calculate pH or Ka for weak monobasic acids using approximations.
Explain limits of the weak acid approximations.
Define a buffer solution.
Describe forming a buffer from a weak acid and its salt, or excess weak acid and strong alkali.
Explain the role of the conjugate acid-base pair in a buffer.
Calculate the pH of a buffer.
Explain control of blood pH by the carbonic acid-hydrogencarbonate buffer.
Sketch and interpret pH titration curves for strong and weak acid-base combinations.
Choose a suitable indicator and explain colour changes using equilibrium shift.
Measure pH using a pH meter.
Define lattice enthalpy and use it as a measure of ionic bond strength.
Construct Born-Haber cycles for simple ionic solids and do related calculations.
Define enthalpy change of solution and of hydration.
Construct enthalpy cycles using solution, hydration and lattice enthalpies and calculate from them.
Explain how ionic charge and radius affect lattice and hydration enthalpies.
Explain entropy as a measure of energy dispersal, greater with more disorder.
Explain differences in entropy between solids, liquids and gases and with changing gas molecule numbers.
Calculate entropy change for a reaction.
Explain that feasibility depends on entropy change, temperature and enthalpy change.
Use the Gibbs equation DG = DH - TDS, with a process feasible when DG is negative.
Explain the limits of DG predictions in terms of kinetics.
Use the terms oxidising agent and reducing agent.
Construct redox equations from half-equations and oxidation numbers.
Interpret and predict electron transfer reactions.
Carry out redox titrations, including Fe2+/MnO4- and I2/S2O3 2-.
Do structured and unstructured redox titration calculations, including unfamiliar systems.
Define standard electrode potential and its measurement with a hydrogen electrode.
Measure cell potentials for metals or non-metals in their ions and for ions of one element in different oxidation states.
Calculate a standard cell potential by combining two electrode potentials.
Predict feasibility from cell potentials and explain limitations from kinetics and concentration.
Apply electrode potential principles to modern storage cells.
Explain how a fuel cell uses a fuel and oxygen to create a voltage, and the changes at each electrode.
Write electron configurations of Period 4 d-block atoms and ions, Sc to Zn.
Identify Ti to Cu as transition elements with an ion having an incomplete d-sub-shell.
Illustrate multiple oxidation states, coloured ions and catalytic behaviour with at least two transition elements.
Explain ligands as coordinate bonds to a metal ion, including monodentate and bidentate ligands.
Use the terms complex ion and coordination number, with octahedral, tetrahedral and square planar examples.
Describe cis-trans and optical isomerism shown by complexes.
Explain the use of cisplatin as an anti-cancer drug and how it binds DNA.
Describe ligand substitution reactions and colour changes for copper and chromium complexes.
Explain the biochemical importance of iron in haemoglobin, including ligand substitution by O2 and CO.
Describe reactions and colour changes of Cu2+, Fe2+, Fe3+, Mn2+ and Cr3+ with sodium hydroxide and ammonia, including precipitates and complex formation in excess.
Describe redox reactions and colour changes between Fe2+ and Fe3+, between Cr3+ and Cr2O7 2-, and for Cu2+/Cu+ with disproportionation of Cu+.
Interpret and predict unfamiliar ligand substitution, precipitation and redox reactions.
Identify anions carbonate, chloride, bromide, iodide and sulfate in an unknown compound.
Identify cations NH4+, Cu2+, Fe2+, Fe3+, Mn2+ and Cr3+ in an unknown compound.
Compare the Kekule and delocalised models of benzene.
Describe evidence for the delocalised model from bond lengths, hydrogenation enthalpy and resistance to reaction.
Name substituted aromatic compounds using IUPAC rules.
Describe nitration, halogenation and Friedel-Crafts reactions of aromatic compounds.
Describe the mechanism of electrophilic substitution for nitration and halogenation.
Explain why benzene resists bromination compared with alkenes.
Interpret unfamiliar electrophilic substitution reactions, including predicting mechanisms.
Explain the weak acidity of phenols, reacting with NaOH but not carbonates.
Describe substitution of phenol with bromine and dilute nitric acid.
Explain why phenol undergoes substitution more easily than benzene.
Describe the 2- and 4-directing effects of OH and NH2 and the 3-directing effect of NO2.
Predict substitution products from directing effects and their importance in synthesis.
Describe oxidation of aldehydes to carboxylic acids with acidified dichromate.
Describe nucleophilic addition of carbonyls with NaBH4 and HCN.
Describe the mechanism of nucleophilic addition to aldehydes and ketones.
Use 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine to detect carbonyls and identify them from derivative melting points.
Use Tollens' reagent to detect aldehydes and distinguish them from ketones.
Explain the water solubility of carboxylic acids through hydrogen bonding.
Describe reactions of carboxylic acids with metals and bases.
Describe esterification of carboxylic acids and acid anhydrides with alcohols.
Describe hydrolysis of esters in hot acid and hot alkali.
Describe forming acyl chlorides from carboxylic acids using SOCl2.
Describe using acyl chlorides to make esters, carboxylic acids and amides.
Explain amine basicity through the nitrogen lone pair and reactions with dilute acids.
Describe preparing aliphatic amines from haloalkanes with ammonia and aromatic amines by reducing nitroarenes.
State the general formula of an alpha-amino acid and its reactions at the carboxylic acid and amine groups.
Draw structures of primary and secondary amides.
Explain optical isomerism as non-superimposable mirror images about a chiral centre.
Identify chiral centres in organic molecules.
Describe condensation polymerisation to form polyesters and polyamides.
Describe acid and base hydrolysis of ester and amide groups in polymers.
Predict repeat units, monomers and the polymerisation type for addition and condensation polymers.
Explain how C-C bond formation increases carbon chain length in synthesis.
Describe forming nitriles from haloalkanes with CN- and from carbonyls with HCN, including mechanisms.
Describe reducing nitriles to amines and hydrolysing them to carboxylic acids.
Describe Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation of aromatic rings.
Prepare organic solids using Quickfit apparatus, distillation and reflux.
Purify solids by reduced pressure filtration, recrystallisation and melting point measurement.
Identify functional groups in a multi-functional molecule and predict its properties and reactions.
Devise multi-stage synthetic routes using transformations between all functional groups studied.
Interpret one-way TLC chromatograms using Rf values.
Interpret gas chromatograms using retention times and component amounts.
Identify alkenes with bromine and haloalkanes with silver nitrate in ethanol.
Identify phenols by weak acidity without reaction with carbonate.
Identify carbonyls with 2,4-DNP and aldehydes with Tollens' reagent.
Identify primary and secondary alcohols and aldehydes with acidified dichromate.
Identify carboxylic acids by reaction with carbonate.
Analyse carbon-13 NMR spectra for carbon environments, their types from chemical shifts, and possible structures.
Analyse high resolution proton NMR for proton environments, their types, relative numbers from integration, and neighbouring protons from the n + 1 rule.
Predict a carbon-13 or proton NMR spectrum for a given molecule.
Explain use of TMS as a standard, deuterated solvents, and D2O exchange for O-H and N-H protons.
Deduce structures from elemental analysis, mass spectra, infrared spectra and NMR spectra.
